title: A Year Of Unexpected Use Cases For Artificial Intelligence (AI)
subtitle: What's worked with AI, a personal year in review for Owen Scott Muir, M.D.
body_html:
I can remember nothing about where I was when ChatGPT was released. I can barely remember any conversation at any party prior to it. Everyone's talking about AI. OK, there's one exception—we have an education secretary who's talking about A1. It's one person talking about steak sauce— and let's not misunderstanding each other, it's an excellent steak sauce— and everybody else is talking about AI.

In the beginning, we all imagined it would be able to do all sorts of work for us. For me, that hasn't been true. There is work AI does for me, but it's become so routine that I don't even think about it. Do you remember medical scribes? Those were people, who were not doctors, who follow doctors around and wrote notes based on what happened in clinical encounters. Doctor then had to check their work, which is its own sort of hell, to figure out what they got wrong.

AI— in my case of tool called MDHub— has replaced the role of scribes in my world. Now, you still need to check its work. If you're going to be checking work, it might as well be work done anywhere you happen to be, generated without having to employ a human scribe to follow you around like a puppy.

If you want to hear what the team at MDhub has to say for themselves, their cofounder is speaking at rapid acting mental health treatment on May 18 in Los Angeles with me!

Get Ramht tickets!

But like every major labor saving innovation, right after it's here, it's common place. The thought of trying to type out a medical note, much less use a pen and paper to write it? Are we living in the goddamn Stone Age? Somebody have a flint? I need to desperately try to start a fire before I freeze to death.

Anything good enough becomes transparent, and we just don't think about it anymore. It is just not a job we do ever onward.

Every time I tell people about this newsletter, they ask me if I use AI to write it. No, I don't, because at least thus far, artificial intelligence is a terrible writer. If you want to have really anodyne writing, writing that sticks the landing on the nexus between completely predictable, plus one too many adjectives per sentence, well, then ChatGPT is here for you. If you wanna make sure that every sentence is both grammatically correct and completely boring? Buckle Up, Sheriff Claude has come to town to Regulate.

There are some used cases for those chatbots that I didn't expect. Things at which it excels, where it's not just replacing a human, but it is doing more than a human could ever do.

I'm speaking of three specific use cases that I hope will knock your socks off…join me for a trip inside my very boring brain.

My kids want to do a bunch of stuff on Vacation, how can we do everything in one day?

The first exceptional use case is vacation planning. When you go somewhere new, nobody, and I mean nobody, can know where everything is. By definition, if it's a new place, you are not going to know where things are in relation to each other.

When we went to Japan, with the kiddos, there were a number of competing priorities. There were also some unexpected constraints. For example, in Osaka, many of the restaurants had rules about not allowing children of a certain age, but they cutoffs for that age were highly variable. We wanted to learn about samurai and ninja (🥷), we wanted to get dressed up in kimonos, and we wanted to go to a guitar store, for dad, and mom wants to make sure she saw fashionable accessories. There was also the desire to have sushi for dinner, but not for lunch. I wanted to see bonsai trees. How could we fit it all into one day? Which bonsai tree exhibit is closest to the relevant guitar store which is on the way to the store where you can look at fashionable accessories that is a hop, skip, and a jump over to Sushi? This requires an array of local knowledge, including geography, restaurant rules and regulations, subway planning! It's enough to make your head spin. But ChatGPT crushed it. We got to do everything we wanted in the day, because it could make a plan that put those things in a rational sequence based on both preferences and relative distance. I was sold, and I'm never going back to vacation without it.

Decorating a new house when you don't care as much about the paint colors as your wife does

I'm in the process of moving! This is a mild to moderately exciting journey, and as my wife likes to point out, you have to select paint and wall paper, because those go on the walls, and you have to do that before you put a bunch of other stuff in a room. About this point, she is not wrong. I also care less about paint than Carlene does. I have opinions, but they're not the kind of opinions I have about healthcare policy, or microphones, or any number of other things about which I care quite a bit.

If only there was a way to interact with my wife, or enable my wife to interact with me, that would allow her to elicit my sentiments about paint, and what paint matched other paints, that was both better informed than my actual self, and more available…with a lower level of…irritability? Or, perhaps, a higher level of engagement about the topic of paint coordination?

Well, thanks for the work of my dear friend who created OwenGPT, there is a robot version of me trained on hundreds of articles I've written on this newsletter, which provides a real time, and impossible to distract simulacrum of myself, with opinions that are closer to my own than I care to admit. One of the things my wife can now do is upload pictures of paint colors, and ask a robot version of her husband what it thinks about that paint, and what other paints would go well with that paint. It does a better job than me. OwenGPT has much more data about paint than the actual Owen, and it doesn't mind being asked questions of any kind, endlessly. It's a great stand in! It allows for feedback in the style of Owen, but without having to be a drain on my actual attention or emotional resources. As an additional bonus, human Owen and Carlene can both be amazed when robot Owen does a good job of selecting what actual Owen would think. Now my wife and I are being amused in the process of selecting paints, instead of frustrated at my lack of paint selection engagement.

What case should I use for these drums?

I am a musician. If you don't believe me, feel free to check out my rendition of Neil Young’s Classic “Cortez the Killer,” right here:

I'm not a very good musician. However, in the process of the aforementioned move, I need to make a drum kit get from one place to another. And I did not know which cases for which drums would fit the drum kit that I had.

This particular drum kit is an electronic drum kit, made by a company called EFnote, and I really didn't want it to get destroyed.

Before I can pull up the graphic of some of that conversation, which by the way did end up with me getting cases for the drums, I just wanna share with you a random selection of things I use ChatGPT for, because I really am as dreadfully boring as you think I am:

Oh my gosh, I am the most boring person you've ever met. Moving on, when you don't know the size of something, the Internet does know the size of that thing. So instead of having to measure, with some prodding, AI can really get you there. It's so much more dynamic version of a buying guide than any human I've ever interacted with, because it just literally knows all the things that are on the Internet—much of which are advertisement or sales material, but which also includes the user manual for almost every product that is anywhere near modern enough to care about.

So there you have it: life-changing use cases for AI? Family trip planning, paint selection, and helping you sort through endless options for drum protection.

It may not be changing the world, but it sure better than looking that stuff up with some kind of archaic search bar in which you have to physically type what you're looking for, and then manually selecting one of a number of websites on which you can try to find that information? Please, what is this, 1997?

Also, I haven't had to write a progress note for about a year. That is priceless!
